617.title: As on a mountain
617.hook: live as if on a mountain; here or there matters little (Meditations 10.15)
617.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use the mountain as a mental vantage point: in the middle of daily friction they picture the wide view, and try to act as they would from there.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Marcus, who trained himself to watch how all things change. Your line was study change.

People dream of the cabin. The mountain view, the quiet, the place where you'll finally be the calm, wise version of yourself. Back in book four, Marcus noted that people seek retreats in the country, by the sea, in the hills, and said you can retreat into yourself instead. In book ten he comes at the same idea from the other side, with a short, strong instruction.
screen: `THE CABIN DREAM.` → `RETREAT INTO YOURSELF.` → `AS ON A MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in George Long's 1862 translation: “Short is the little which remains to thee of life. Live as on a mountain.” It makes no difference, Marcus goes on, whether a person lives here or there, as long as they live everywhere in the world as a citizen of one great city. The mountain isn't a place you move to. It's a way of standing: above the noise, seeing far, not tangled in every small quarrel of the town below. Let people see, he says, let them know, a real human being living by nature. And then a hard line: if they can't stand him, let them kill him, because that's better than living the way they live. It's the voice of a man who knew public life could be dangerous, and who wanted to be the same in public as in private. So why the mountain and not the cabin? The cabin promises you'll be different somewhere else. Marcus says the shortness of life means there's no time to wait for the right setting. The height has to come with you, into the office, the kitchen, the commute. Here or there matters little. What you carry matters a great deal.

618.title: Is it this you'd miss?
618.hook: afraid of death? is it this particular errand you'd miss? (Meditations 10.29)
618.tomorrow: Let no one say it truly
618.howItsDone: Some readers of the Meditations pause during routine tasks and ask Marcus's question, which helps them see trivial worries at their real size and notice which parts of the day they truly value.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was George Long, whose translation says live as on a mountain. Your line was here or there matters little.

You're refolding towels. Answering the fourteenth email about the same meeting. Scrolling past a video you've already seen three times. Then someone leans in and asks: if you had to leave this life today, is this what you'd miss? It's an odd question over a basket of laundry, and an odd one to ask yourself at all. But Marcus asks it in book ten of the Meditations, and he asks it of everything he does.
screen: `REFOLDING TOWELS.` → `THE FOURTEENTH EMAIL.` → `IS IT THIS YOU'D MISS?`

segments.voice: In every single thing you do, Marcus writes, stop and ask yourself: is death terrible because it takes this away from me? That's the whole entry. He's pointing the question at his own fear of dying. Much of what fills an hour isn't something we'd miss. If death is frightening because it would take away this errand, this complaint, this scroll, then the fear is smaller than it seemed. But the question cuts the other way too. If you look at what you're doing and the honest answer is, no, I wouldn't miss this, then why does so much of the day go to it? The question that loosens the fear of death also sorts the hours of a life. Some things pass the test easily: a long talk at the kitchen table, the evening walk, the work that matters to you. And this isn't contempt. Marcus isn't saying ordinary life is worthless. A few entries earlier, he told himself to be content with what is given now. Towels still need folding. The point isn't to despise the errand. It's to see it at its real size, so it doesn't carry more weight than it should, in your fears or in your hours. And Marcus leaves it as he found it: a question, asked again in every act.

619.title: Let no one say it truly
619.hook: let no one be able to say truly that you aren't simple or good (Meditations 10.32)
619.howItsDone: People who use this passage often answer criticism by first asking whether it's true, and if any part is, by quietly changing that part rather than arguing.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was second edge: Marcus's question, is it this I'd miss, loosens the fear of death and sorts the hours. Your line was is it this.

Someone says something about you behind your back. Selfish, they say, or fake, or lazy. It stings, and soon you're arguing with them in your head, in the shower, on the drive. But there's a quieter question under the sting: is it true? Marcus doesn't tell himself to stop people talking. He tells himself something harder, and much more in his control.
screen: `SAID BEHIND YOUR BACK.` → `ARGUING IN THE SHOWER.` → `LET NO ONE SAY IT TRULY.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Let no one be able to say truthfully of you, Marcus writes, that you are not simple, or not good. Let anyone who thinks that of you be a liar. Second, the shift. He isn't trying to control what people say. People will say what they say. He's trying to control whether it's true. You can't stop the rumor. You can make it false. Third, it's in your power. All of this, he writes, is up to you. Who can stop you from being good and simple? No one. Others can mislabel you, but they can't make the label stick to the person you actually are. Fourth, the test. When a remark lands, there are two questions. Is it true? If it isn't, it's their mistake, and you can let it go. If it is, even a little, you've been handed a free piece of information, and the work is to make it false. Either way, the energy goes into living, not defending. And notice his pair of words: simple and good, the same pair book ten opened with, when he asked his soul whether it would ever be good and simple. A few pages later, he's still working on it.

620.title: Glad at your going
620.hook: no one is so lucky that no one will be glad at their death, not even Marcus (Meditations 10.36)
620.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus sometimes use this passage to loosen the sense of being indispensable, picturing life going on without them while resolving to stay kind to everyone around them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was two questions: is it true, and if so, how do I make it false. Your line was let it be false.

The last day at a job: the cake, the card, the kind speeches. And somewhere in the room, someone quietly relieved you're going. Maybe you never knew, and maybe that was for the best. Marcus, emperor of Rome, writes in book ten that it would be the same at his own death: someone standing by would be glad. Not because he was cruel. Just because that's how people are.
screen: `THE LAST DAY AT A JOB.` → `SOMEONE QUIETLY RELIEVED.` → `GLAD AT YOUR GOING.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. No one is so fortunate, Marcus writes, that when they're dying there won't be some standing by who welcome what's happening. Second, even the good. Suppose the person was good and wise. Won't someone still say under their breath: at last we can breathe again, free of this schoolmaster? He was never harsh with any of us, but I always felt him quietly judging us. That, Marcus says, is what's said of a good man. Third, and me? Then he turns it on himself. In my case, he says, there are many more reasons people would be glad to be rid of me. Even the companions he has worked for, prayed for and cared for will want him gone, hoping to gain something by it. Humbling words, from a man who ruled the Roman world. Fourth, how to hold it. Not with bitterness. Don't, for this reason, go away less kindly disposed toward them, Marcus says. Keep your own character: friendly, well-meaning, gentle. Let go easily, not as if you were being torn away. So the thought is a lightness, not a wound. If even the gentle schoolmaster can be resented, anyone can. You aren't the center of everyone's world, and that's a kind of relief. Hold your importance lightly, and keep being kind.

621.title: My own fruit
621.hook: the rational soul sees itself, shapes itself, and gathers its own fruit (Meditations 11.1)
621.howItsDone: Some readers of the Meditations end the day with a short, honest look at themselves, naming one good thing they grew and one thing to shape differently tomorrow.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was schoolmaster: even a good, gentle person leaves someone relieved. Your line was lightly.

An apple tree grows an apple, and someone else eats it. A cow makes milk, and someone else drinks it. A vine grows grapes for somebody's table. Plants and animals, Marcus says, bear fruit that others enjoy. Book eleven of the Meditations opens with him noticing one kind of fruit that's different, one harvest that stays with the one who grows it.
screen: `AN APPLE FOR SOMEONE ELSE.` → `BOOK ELEVEN OPENS.` → `MY OWN FRUIT.`

segments.voice: First, the mirror. The reasoning soul, Marcus says, sees itself, examines itself, and shapes itself into whatever it chooses. No plant can look at itself and decide to grow differently. We can. Second, the fruit. The fruit it bears, he says, it gathers for itself. A tree's fruit and an animal's yield are enjoyed by others. But the fruit of a well-lived life, steadiness, kindness, clear sight, belongs to the one who grew it. You don't have to wait for someone else to taste it. Third, whole at every point. A dance or a play, Marcus says, is left incomplete if it's cut off partway. But the soul reaches its own end wherever life stops. Each act done well is whole in itself, so at any moment it can say: I have what is my own. Fourth, the wide view. The soul ranges over the whole universe and the emptiness around it, stretches into endless time, and sees that those who come after us will see nothing new. A person of forty, he adds, with any understanding at all, has in a sense seen everything that has been and will be: the same patterns keep coming round. And closer to home, look honestly at yourself, and the harvest is already yours.

622.title: Already rewarded
622.hook: have I done something for the common good? then I've been rewarded (Meditations 11.4)
622.howItsDone: People who take this note seriously often do small, unannounced things for shared spaces and neighbors, and treat the doing itself as the point rather than waiting for thanks.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Marcus, and the reasoning soul that gathers its own fruit. Your line was gather your own harvest.

Somewhere in most of us there's a receipt book. Drove her to the airport: one slip. Covered his shift: another. Remembered the birthday, listened for an hour on the phone, lent the ladder and got it back with a dent. Nobody asked us to keep it. We keep it anyway, and every slip says the same thing underneath: you owe me. Marcus wrote a short note in book eleven that closes the book before the first slip is written.
screen: `A RECEIPT BOOK IN YOUR HEAD.` → `EVERY SLIP SAYS: YOU OWE ME.` → `ALREADY REWARDED.`

segments.voice: First, the note. Have I done something for the common good? Marcus asks. Then I've been rewarded. Keep this always at hand, he adds, and never stop. Second, why it's already paid. In book nine he put it sharply: wanting a return for a kindness is like an eye demanding a fee for seeing, or feet for walking. Seeing is what an eye is for. For Marcus, working with and for others is what a person is for, so the doing is the payment. Third, one letter. In book seven he plays on two Greek words that differ by a single letter. Melos means a limb, like an arm or a hand. Meros means a part, a piece, like one brick in a pile. Think of yourself as only a part of humankind, he says, and you don't yet love people from the heart; you do good because it's proper, as a duty. Think of yourself as a limb of the one body, and doing good becomes doing good to yourself. A hand doesn't send the arm an invoice. Fourth, why it's freeing. If the reward is in the doing, no one can cheat you or ignore you out of it. The account is settled the moment you act. Thanks is still welcome. You just aren't waiting for it.

623.title: Kind to everyone
623.hook: if someone despises me, that's theirs; mine is to be kind to all (Meditations 11.13)
623.howItsDone: People who draw on this passage often separate another person's dislike from their own conduct, checking whether they've given real cause, and then offering ordinary kindness regardless.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was already rewarded: done for the common good, already paid. Your line was no invoice.

There's someone who doesn't like you. A relative, a neighbor, a coworker who rolls their eyes when you talk. It's tempting to make it a project: win them over, dislike them right back, or make sure everyone knows who started it. Marcus asks it plainly in book eleven: does someone despise me? Then he splits the problem neatly in two, and keeps only one half.
screen: `SOMEONE WHO DOESN'T LIKE YOU.` → `WIN THEM, OR DISLIKE THEM BACK?` → `KIND TO EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: First, the split. Does someone despise me? Marcus writes. That's for them to see to. Mine is to make sure I'm not found doing or saying anything that deserves contempt. Does someone hate me? Their concern. Mine is to be gentle and kind toward everyone, this person included. Second, ready to show them. He adds that he'll be ready to show that very person where they've gone wrong, not by scolding, and not by making a show of his own patience, but nobly and honestly. Third, Phocion. He gives an example: like the great Phocion, unless Phocion was only pretending. Phocion was an Athenian general condemned to death by his own city. Plutarch tells that before he died, someone asked whether he had a message for his son, and he said to tell him to bear no grudge against the Athenians. Marcus admires it, then adds a dry footnote: unless it was an act. Fourth, the week, looking back. As on a mountain. Is it this. Let it be false. Lightly. My own fruit. No invoice. And now, theirs, and mine. Several of them draw a line between what belongs to others and what belongs to you, and put your effort on your own side of it. Their opinion is theirs. Your kindness is yours.
